authors: Alex Reinhart (not printed in the PDF text; from the caller's note)

question: How should one interpret p values, significance tests and confidence intervals when judging differences between experimental groups?
contributions: Explains p value as a measure of surprise under the null, not effect size or importance
Shows p depends on experimental design (stopping rule)
Argues for confidence intervals over p values

results.claim: A 12-question true/false test with 9 correct gives p = 0.073 under random guessing (binomial, fixed n=12): not significant at 0.05.
results.setup: Null: guessing with equal probability; stopping rule: ask 12 questions; binomial distribution

results.claim: The same data (9 right, 3 wrong) under an 'ask until 3 wrong' stopping rule gives p = 0.033, significant at 0.05: the p value depends on experimental design.
results.setup: Same data; negative binomial; sampling stops at 3 wrong answers

results.claim: In experimental psychology journals 97% of papers involve significance testing but only about 10% report confidence intervals.
results.metric: share of papers using significance testing
results.setup: Experimental psychology research journals; chapter footnote 8 (reference list not in the PDF); ~10% report CIs

results.claim: 89% of Nature articles report p values without any confidence intervals or effect sizes.
results.setup: Nature; chapter footnote 9 (reference list not in the PDF)

results.claim: Illustrative interval: drug cuts average cold length by 36 hours, 95% CI 24 to 48 hours.
results.quote: reduces the average length of a cold by

results.claim: Illustrative interval: a trial's CI of 15 to 25 percent symptom reduction excludes zero, so it is significant, and importance is judged clinically.
If you test on 10 million patients it is very unlikely all get shorter colds by luck; with one patient it is unsurprising (intuition behind p).
The 0.05 threshold has no special logical or statistical basis; it is convention.
A single experiment has no false positive rate; the rate belongs to the procedure (alpha), so p = 0.032 does not mean a 3.2% false positive rate.
results.quote: does not have a false positive rate

limits: Chapter only: no reference list, so footnotes 1-12 (Thompson, Neyman-Pearson, Rothman, journal surveys) are not checkable here.
Examples are hypothetical (cold medicine, 12-question quiz); no original experiment.
Does not cover multiple comparisons, power, or base-rate issues (later chapters).
Journal survey figures (97%, 10%, 89%) are old and from other work.
practices: Treat p as a measure of surprise, not of effect size or importance (p.9).
Do not equate statistical significance with practical significance (p.9).
Do not read a statistically insignificant result as no effect; it may need more data (p.9).
Decide the alpha before the experiment; do not report a single result's p as its false positive rate (p.12).
Write results as confidence intervals instead of p values when you can (p.13).
Check whether a CI includes zero to test significance, and if the CI is too wide collect more data (p.13).
Judge the importance of an interval with domain knowledge (p.13).
Journal editors can drive reporting change, as Rothman did (p.14).

terms.definition: The probability, under the assumption that there is no true effect or no true difference, of collecting data that shows a difference equal to or more extreme than what you actually observed.
Answers: 'Even if my medication were completely ineffective, what are the chances my experiment would have produced the observed outcome?'
The predefined rate at which false positives occur under the Neyman-Pearson procedure; reject the null whenever p < alpha.
False positive: concluding there is an effect when there isn't; false negative: failing to notice a real effect.
A hypothesis that there is no effect; paired with an alternative such as 'the effect is greater than zero'.
Combines a point estimate with the uncertainty in that estimate; of 100 identical experiments about 95 of the 95% intervals include the true value.
